summary: Initial phone screen for Backend Inference Engineer. Lee has 5+ years in infra and ML serving, previously at OptiScale and a startup doing quantized transformer serving. Strong systems background; moderate familiarity with CUDA/Triton and kernel-level profiling. Agreed next step is a take-home assignment and onsite loop.
transcript:
[00:00] Aisha: Hi Lee, thanks for taking the call. We're on a quick 40 minute screen, I'm Aisha, hiring manager for the inference infra team, this is Carlos from the serving runtime team.
[00:09] Lee: Thanks, nice to meet you both.
[00:12] Carlos: Hey Lee. quick housekeeping, can you confirm you're okay with us recording?
[00:16] Lee: Yes that's fine.
[00:18] Aisha: Great, so we'll spend first 10 minutes on background, then some technical discussion—latency/cost tradeoffs, quantization—then wrap with next steps. Sound good?
[00:27] Lee: Sounds good.
[00:30] Aisha: Can you give a quick run through your last two roles? high level, what you owned and what scale you saw.
[00:38] Lee: Sure. most recently I was at OptiScale, an inference startup, I led the runtime team for two years. We shipped a microservices-based inference platform, supporting seq lengths up to 2k and p99 latencies in the 80-200ms range depending on model. Prior to that I was at a startup called MapMorph where I focused on model compilers and kernel interfaces—basically bridging pytorch models into lower level kernels, worked a lot with TVM and some Triton.
[01:05] Carlos: When you say p99 80-200ms, what's the typical hardware? gpus? v100?
[01:10] Lee: We had mixed infra—A100 for production. Some on-prem NVIDIAs for cost testing. We used quantized int8 for smaller models and mixed precision for big ones. We also had a dedicated pool for latency-sensitive customers.
[01:22] Aisha: Great. can you talk about a specific perf regression you chased and how you triaged it?
[01:28] Lee: Yeah, one time we saw p95 spike after a model update; it was due to a change in attention masking that increased KV cache misses and caused more memory copies. I instrumented the KV cache paths, added better prefetching, reduced memcpys by reusing buffers and changed the scheduler so large batched requests weren't scheduled onto the low-latency pool. Ended up cutting p95 back down by ~40%.
[01:51] Carlos: Nice. curious—what tools did you use to profile? nvprof? nsight? tracers?
[01:56] Lee: Mostly Nsight and CUPTI for kernel timelines, some homegrown tracer to correlate request ids through the stack. We also used perf and eBPF for host-level bottlenecks.
[02:07] Aisha: Do you have hands-on with kernel development or mainly orchestration and scheduling?
[02:12] Lee: A bit of both. I wrote some CUDA kernels for custom attention variants during MapMorph days. More recently I focused on orchestration, batching strategies, and cache coherence.
[02:22] Carlos: How do you think about batching policy—what parameters do you tune and how do you decide dynamic vs fixed batching?
[02:29] Lee: I tune max batch size, latency SLO thresholds, per-worker concurrency, and an arrival window. For latency-sensitive routes we go with conservative max batch and small arrival window, plus prefix caching. For throughput routes, higher max batch and allow more elastic waiting. Also I use adaptive policies that shrink window when latency approaches SLO.
[02:51] Carlos: Redwood has a prefix/K-V cache and continuous batching approach—any gotchas you've seen with caching across model variants?
[02:58] Lee: Yeah, invalidation complexity. If customer pins model versions or you have multiple quantized variants, the cache keys need to include model artifact id and quantization tag. Otherwise stale cache returns are a headache. Also serialization format differences between kernels can break reuse.
[03:15] Aisha: Good point. Have you worked on model fallback or graceful degradation strategies?
[03:20] Lee: We implemented automatic fallback to a lower-capacity but compatible model family when latency or GPU OOMs happen. It was rule-based initially, then we layered in a small RL policy to pick fallback based on request characteristics.
[03:30] Carlos: Interesting. on quantization—what's your experience with int8 vs 4-bit, PTQ vs QAT? any quality surprises?
[03:37] Lee: Mostly PTQ for inferencing at scale; we used outlier clipping and per-channel scales to avoid big quality drops. For tight SLO customers we tried QAT but it was heavier to maintain across rollouts. 4-bit was promising but often needed per-layer calibration and sometimes caused hallucination-like errors in LLM outputs if not tuned per task.
[03:58] Aisha: Do you have experience with on-prem deployments or VPC/private modes? security/compliance?
[04:04] Lee: Yes, we were contracted to run private installs for a healthcare customer—had to integrate with their KMS, enable FIPS mode in some libs, and ship audit logs. We ran into network restrictions and had to bundle a lightweight bootstrap for models.
[04:18] Carlos: How comfortable are you debugging live infra issues—like a sudden latency spike in prod during a deploy?
[04:24] Lee: Comfortable—I've done on-call and incident leading. First step is to isolate whether it's infra, model, or client changes, check metrics (cpu,gpu util, queue latencies), correlate with recent deploys, then roll back or route around. I lean toward circuit-breakers and canaries to limit blast radius.
[04:42] Aisha: Some behavioral—how do you work with product and SRE teams?
[04:45] Lee: I prefer regular syncs, clear SLO definitions, and runbooks. I also love pairing sessions to transfer operational knowledge.
[04:52] Carlos: Quick coding question—how would you implement a lightweight prefix cache for requests? high level.
[04:57] Lee: I would use an in-memory LRU per-worker with a sharded keyspace by prefix hash to avoid hotspots. Keys include model id, prefix token hash, and quantization tag. Eviction policy tuned by hit-rate targets. For cross-worker reuse, either a shared memcached layer or a hot-keys replication protocol, but that adds complexity.
[05:20] Carlos: What about KV cache memory pressure—how do you safely reclaim?
[05:24] Lee: Evict cold keys, compress long KV entries, and use soft-limits to trigger adaptive batching reduction. In OOM cases, prefer dropping batched background jobs before latency-critical ones.
[05:35] Aisha: Any questions for us about the role or team?
[05:38] Lee: Yeah, how big is the team, and what's the mix of infra vs model infra work?
[05:42] Aisha: The team is around 18 engineers spread across runtime, orchestration, and ops. This role skews infra/runtime—building kernels, batching, and some assembler glue.
[05:53] Lee: What's the expected ramp and first 90-day goals?
[05:56] Aisha: First 30 — onboard, core infra; 60 — take ownership of a component (e.g., batching or cache layer); 90 — lead a perf improvement project.
[06:06] Carlos: Two quick clarification points: have you used Triton inference server in prod?
[06:11] Lee: Limited exposure—I did performance integrations and wrote custom backends once, but most of my production work was custom runtime.
[06:19] Carlos: And are you comfortable with C++ and some CUDA?
[06:22] Lee: Yes, C++ is daily; CUDA I'm comfortable with kernel debugging and small kernels, not large shared libraries maintenance.
[06:31] Aisha: One more—previous managers often ask about remote collaboration, can you give example of cross-team project?
[06:36] Lee: Sure, I led a cross-team initiative to standardize telemetry across infra and model teams—built a lightweight trace header and unified schema, this reduced mean time to detect regressions.
[06:48] Aisha: Awesome. wrap up: we'll send a take-home that exercises batching/latency tradeoffs and a small profiling task. Should take 4-6 hours. Is that timeline ok?
[06:58] Lee: Yes that's fine.
[07:00] Aisha: Any final questions?
[07:02] Lee: None right now.
[07:03] Carlos: Thanks Lee.
[07:05] Aisha: We'll follow up with next steps — thanks for your time.
[07:08] Lee: Thanks, bye.

Notes: transcript has some minor auto-transcription errors (e.g., "K-V" sometimes shows as "K B cache", and "Ku-bear-nates" for k8s in one spot) and occasional missing punctuation. End of recording.
